notes: Plan repairs: replaced short-lived-secret-leak-window with mounted-secret-api-permission-reduction to test Kubernetes credential exposure; incomplete-sbom-dependency-blind-spot with sbom-format-metadata-completeness for verified Trivy metadata requirements; virtual-control-plane-data-plane-gap with virtual-control-plane-cluster-policy-isolation to avoid repeating worker isolation; and istio-sidecar-mtls-proxy-boundary with istio-service-identity-impersonation-check to avoid repeating TLS termination.

cards.statement: An admitted Pod exposes its mounted Secret to its creator despite RBAC restrictions on that user's direct Secret reads.
cards.explanation: A Pod creator chooses code that consumes the mounted Secret, exposing its value through workload access rather than direct API reads.

cards.statement: Removing a retired etcd member from a Kubernetes cluster also sanitizes the Secret data on its durable storage.
cards.explanation: Retired etcd storage can retain Secret data; sanitize its durable media separately.
cards.misconception: Retiring an etcd member also erases its stored Secrets.

cards.statement: Mounting a needed Secret lets operators avoid granting its Pod's ServiceAccount namespace-wide Secret API read access.
cards.explanation: Secret mounts provide needed values while keeping the Pod's ServiceAccount outside a broader Secret-read permission grant.

cards.statement: Under default Linux container isolation, a compromised sidecar reads a Secret mounted solely into its sibling.
cards.explanation: Secret mounts grant container-specific access. Restrict them to containers that need the credentials.
cards.misconception: Siblings inherit Secret volume access from sharing a Pod.

cards.statement: With Secrets encrypted in etcd, an application's crash-dump logs can still expose Secret environment variables.
cards.explanation: Secret values in environment variables can enter crash dumps and logs after the application receives plaintext.

cards.statement: Kubernetes Secret encryption at rest can configure TLS automatically on etcd's peer connections.
cards.explanation: etcd peer connections require their own TLS configuration; Kubernetes data encryption settings do not enable peer TLS.
cards.misconception: Secret encryption at rest automatically configures etcd peer TLS.

cards.statement: With KMS v2 configured, the API server encrypts Secret data locally while a remote KMS protects its key material.
cards.explanation: The API server handles payload encryption with derived DEKs; the external KMS protects key material instead of receiving Secret payloads.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: With KMS v2, revoking remote KEK access can immediately stop API server decryption using cached plaintext key material.
cards.explanation: KMS v2's cached plaintext keys support decryption during remote KMS outages.
cards.misconception: Revoking remote KMS access invalidates cached plaintext keys.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: For KMS v2, the API server rejects an Encrypt response whose key_id differs from the plugin's Status key_id.
cards.explanation: KMS v2 treats Status as the authoritative key ID; conflicting Encrypt responses mark the plugin unhealthy.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: For an API server using a configured KMS v2 plugin, rotating the remote KEK requires restarting that API server.
cards.explanation: The API server detects KMS v2 key rotation through Status polling and keeps running during the change.
cards.misconception: KMS v2 remote-key rotation requires an API server restart.

source.title: Using a KMS provider for data encryption

cards.statement: With ordinary containers sharing a worker node, namespace separation confines a container escape to its tenant.
cards.explanation: Namespaces group API resources and policies; they do not separate a shared node's kernel.
cards.misconception: Namespace boundaries contain host access gained through a container escape.

cards.statement: A tenant's virtual control plane isolates cluster-wide admission webhooks from other tenants' API configurations.
cards.explanation: Separate tenant control planes avoid conflicts over cluster-scoped objects such as admission webhooks, giving tenants independent API policy configuration.

cards.statement: Dedicated tenant nodes prevent lateral movement through Kubernetes credentials exposed on a compromised node.
cards.explanation: An attacker can use node-exposed credentials against shared cluster services to reach other tenants.
cards.misconception: Dedicated worker nodes confine the reach of their exposed Kubernetes credentials.

cards.statement: A configured VM-backed sandbox runtime adds a kernel boundary between a tenant's workload and its Linux host.
cards.explanation: A VM-backed sandbox gives the workload a separate kernel, adding isolation beyond ordinary containers' shared host kernel.

cards.statement: When a RuntimeClass handler is unavailable, kubelet can start its Pod with the node's default runtime handler.
cards.explanation: A Pod fails when its selected RuntimeClass handler is unavailable; kubelet does not substitute the default handler.
cards.misconception: RuntimeClass handler failures silently fall back to the node's default runtime.

cards.statement: With IPsec encryption enabled, Cilium encrypts cross-node traffic between known Cilium-managed Pod endpoints.
cards.explanation: Cilium IPsec protects traffic between its managed Pod endpoints on different nodes.

cards.statement: With WireGuard encryption enabled, Cilium-managed Pods exchange same-node traffic through an encrypted tunnel.
cards.explanation: Cilium leaves same-node traffic outside its WireGuard tunnel; local host access already exposes the plaintext.
cards.misconception: Cilium WireGuard encryption also tunnels local traffic between Pods on one node.

cards.statement: With Cilium IPsec encryption enabled, a node capture can show decrypted inner traffic alongside encrypted ESP packets.
cards.explanation: The host recirculates decrypted IPsec packets for processing. A capture can include plaintext after decryption alongside outer ESP packets.

cards.statement: In Istio sidecar mode, PERMISSIVE lets server Envoy upgrade a plaintext client's connection to mutual TLS.
cards.explanation: PERMISSIVE accepts plaintext alongside mutual TLS. A client sending plaintext keeps that connection unencrypted.
cards.misconception: PERMISSIVE upgrades directly received plaintext connections rather than accepting plaintext.

cards.statement: In Istio sidecar mode, client Envoy can reject a server's valid mesh certificate for a mismatched HTTP service.
cards.explanation: Istio's client Envoy checks whether the server's ServiceAccount identity is authorized to run the target service. A trusted mesh certificate alone does not establish that association.

cards.statement: Kubernetes recommends ephemeral debug containers as an alternative to packaging debug utilities in production images.
cards.explanation: Keep the production image focused on the application and its dependencies. An ephemeral debug container provides troubleshooting tools separately.

cards.statement: Node OS updates can patch a minimal image's retained libraries through the node's package manager.
cards.explanation: An image packages its application and system libraries separately from the host. Fix a packaged library in a new image and recreate the container from that image.
cards.misconception: Patching a node's operating system also patches libraries packaged inside its container images.

source.title: Containers — Container images and host independence

cards.statement: Cosign applies an expected-builder policy during a build attestation's basic signature verification.
cards.explanation: Signature verification authenticates the attestation. Enforcing a required builder needs policy validation of the attestation's predicate.
cards.misconception: Verifying a build attestation's signature also evaluates deployment rules about its build process.

cards.statement: With OS and library detection enabled, Trivy's image SBOM limits coverage to operating-system packages.
cards.explanation: Trivy's image SBOM includes detected operating-system packages and supported language dependencies. An OS package list alone misses part of that dependency inventory.
cards.misconception: Image SBOM inventory covers operating-system packages but leaves language dependencies to another report.

source.title: SBOM — Supported packages and SPDX relationships

cards.statement: Trivy's SPDX relationships show investigators which inventoried packages depend on a suspect library.
cards.explanation: SPDX dependency relationships connect an inventoried library to the packages that need it, helping investigators trace where that dependency enters the image.

source.title: SBOM — Supported packages and SPDX relationships

cards.statement: Trivy can find new vulnerabilities in an unchanged SBOM when it rescans with updated vulnerability data.
cards.explanation: Trivy matches inventoried package versions against its vulnerability database. New advisory data can change the findings for the same inventory.

source.title: Trivy SBOM command — Vulnerability scanning and database updates

cards.statement: An SBOM's valid SPDX structure establishes the package metadata Trivy needs for accurate vulnerability matching.
cards.explanation: Trivy relies on custom SBOM properties for accurate scanning. A valid SPDX document can still omit metadata needed for reliable package identification.
cards.misconception: A valid SBOM format guarantees the metadata quality needed for accurate vulnerability scanning.

source.title: SBOM scanning — External SBOM metadata limitation

cards.statement: By default, Trivy returns a success exit status to CI after an image scan reports vulnerability findings.
cards.explanation: A CI job that treats scanner success as approval can publish an image with findings. Set a failure exit status for the chosen policy and make the pipeline honor it.
cards.volatilityNote: Trivy's default exit-code behavior is a project CLI default that could change across releases.

cards.statement: Shared node-level registry credentials let the kubelet enforce tenant-specific access to private images.
cards.explanation: Pods on a node can access private registries authorized by shared node credentials. Namespace separation does not give those credentials a separate authorization scope for each tenant.
cards.misconception: Shared registry credentials on a node preserve separate image access rights for individual tenants.

cards.statement: An attacker controlling a CI system's OIDC identity can obtain Sigstore certificates under that identity.
cards.explanation: Sigstore can issue certificates to a compromised OIDC identity. Protecting the CI identity remains part of the signing trust boundary.

source.title: Sigstore Threat Model — OIDC account compromise

cards.statement: An installed policy-controller with opt-in webhooks skips registry checks for namespaces outside its opt-in selection.
cards.explanation: An unselected namespace sits outside policy-controller validation, so namespace selection defines the registry policy's coverage.

cards.statement: A registry policy's static pass authority verifies the signer of an image it admits through policy-controller.
cards.explanation: policy-controller's static pass authority accepts matching images without checking their signatures.
cards.misconception: Registry allowance also proves a trusted signer.

cards.statement: A Pod's image digest pin prevents a registry tag change from substituting different container code.
cards.explanation: A digest identifies fixed image content. The kubelet uses that content even if a registry moves a tag.

cards.statement: A valid image signature establishes that the workload is safe for production use in a Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: Software safety needs a separate assessment; signature verification does not evaluate the workload's behavior.
cards.misconception: A valid signature proves production safety.

cards.statement: Cosign keyless verification checks an expected certificate identity together with its expected OIDC issuer.
cards.explanation: An authorization policy identifies both the intended signer and the identity provider trusted to authenticate that signer.

cards.statement: Cosign validates the signed image digest against its target image when default claim checks remain enabled.
cards.explanation: Cosign's claim checks compare the image digest in the signature payload with the image being verified.

cards.statement: In an opted-in namespace, policy-controller automatically pins admitted image tags to resolved digests.
cards.explanation: policy-controller's tag resolution ties deployment to the content evaluated during admission.

cards.statement: In an opted-in namespace, policy-controller rejects violations of its sole matching policy configured in warn mode.
cards.explanation: With a sole matching policy in warn mode, policy-controller admits noncompliant images and returns a warning.
cards.misconception: Policy warnings block image admission.

cards.statement: During validation, policy-controller admits an image that passes one matching enforce policy and fails another.
cards.explanation: policy-controller combines matching enforcing ClusterImagePolicy resources with AND; admission requires satisfying them.
cards.misconception: Matching image policies are alternatives.

cards.statement: Cosign invalidates a historically valid keyless image signature when its signing certificate expires.
cards.explanation: Cosign uses a trusted timestamp to evaluate certificate validity at signing time, preserving later verification.
cards.misconception: Certificate expiry invalidates historical signatures.
